name: Carlos Alcaraz

techniqueNotes.note: Semi-western grip with an explosive unit turn, the racquet tip pointing forward in the take-back and a deep wrist lag before a whip-like acceleration; he hits mostly from open and semi-open stances and often leaves the ground from the leg drive.

Disguises the forehand drop shot by using the same full forehand preparation, then slipping to a continental grip at the last moment and carving under the ball with soft hands, usually when the opponent is pinned deep behind the baseline.
Moves forward constantly behind big forehands, split-stepping around the service line and punching volleys with a continental grip and short backswing; also uses serve-and-volley as a surprise play.

lesson: Combine power with variety: the threat of the big forehand is what makes the drop shot work.

name: Jannik Sinner

techniqueNotes.note: Prepares with an early unit turn and a compact take-back, then drives through the ball with a flat swing, a contact point well in front and a long extension; clean timing rather than muscle produces some of the highest backhand speeds on tour.
Semi-western grip with a compact modern take-back and pronounced racquet lag; he stays balanced with a wide base, keeps his head still through contact and takes the ball early from on the baseline.
His background as a skier shows in a low, wide stance and the ability to slide into open-stance shots on both wings on hard courts while staying balanced.

lesson: Clean timing, early contact and balance generate more pace than swinging harder.

name: Daniil Medvedev

techniqueNotes.note: Hits an unusually flat two-hander with a short, low take-back and very little topspin, meeting the ball with a firm, linear swing so it skids low through the court and is hard to attack.
Stands several meters behind the baseline to return, giving himself time for a full groundstroke swing; he returns deep and central, then uses his reach and movement to work back into the point.
From 1.98 m he uses a quick, simple motion with a relatively low toss and hits flat serves close to the lines, earning many free points.

lesson: Depth and low, flat consistency can dismantle opponents even without textbook-looking strokes.

name: Alexander Zverev

techniqueNotes.note: Widely considered one of the best two-handers in the game: early shoulder turn, straight arms at contact, and a drive through the ball with the left hand dominant, which lets him hit down the line with pace from almost any position.
At 1.98 m he hits first serves regularly above 220 km/h using a high toss, a deep knee bend and full upward extension into contact; the height of contact gives a steep angle into the box.
Uses a semi-western grip with a larger loop and tends to hit with more topspin and net clearance from further back, the more conservative wing of his game.

lesson: A technically sound two-handed backhand can be both your steadiest shot and your biggest weapon.

name: Stefanos Tsitsipas

techniqueNotes.note: Runs around his backhand to hit a heavy inside-out forehand, with a fluid high take-back, full shoulder rotation and an aggressive step forward into the court after contact.

Hits the one-hander with an eastern backhand grip, a full shoulder turn and a long, flowing follow-through with the chest staying sideways; he blends in a knifing slice to stay in rallies when the ball gets high.
Follows serves and forehands to net often, using a continental grip and a forward-moving split step, closing the net to cut off angles.

lesson: Build points around your best shot and move forward to finish them.

name: Casper Ruud

techniqueNotes.note: Uses a strong semi-western grip and a steep low-to-high swing to produce some of the heaviest topspin on tour; he gives the ball high net clearance and lets it kick up out of the opponent's strike zone.
Moves around the backhand with small adjustment steps to hit forehands from the backhand corner, then recovers with a crossover step; clay-style point construction built on patience and position.
Relies on a heavy kick serve with a toss over the head and a brush up the back of the ball, setting up the forehand as the first shot of the rally.

lesson: Heavy topspin with high net clearance makes you consistent and hard to attack at the same time.

name: Taylor Fritz

techniqueNotes.note: At 1.96 m he uses a smooth motion with a platform stance and full extension up to contact, hitting flat serves up to around 240 km/h and mixing in a heavy slice out wide on the deuce side.
Hits a flat, penetrating forehand with a semi-western grip and a fairly straight hitting arm, excelling at sharp cross-court angles and at stepping in on the first ball after the serve.
Drives a flat, compact two-hander, particularly effective cross-court at sharp angles to open the court.

lesson: Practice the serve and the first shot after it as a single pattern.

name: Andrey Rublev

techniqueNotes.note: Swings with maximum racquet-head speed on nearly every forehand: a fast compact take-back, strong hip rotation and a whip through contact, with busy adjustment steps beforehand so the ball is always in his strike zone.
Very active feet between shots, constantly repositioning to hit forehands from the middle and backhand side of the court and recovering quickly to the center.
Hits a flat, early two-hander from on the baseline to keep the tempo high and deny opponents time.

lesson: Fast feet put the ball in your strike zone so you can swing freely.

name: Ben Shelton

techniqueNotes.note: A lefty motion with a very deep knee bend and a huge vertical leg drive, launching up into contact; he has hit serves around 240 km/h and uses the lefty slice out wide on the ad court and a high-bouncing kick.
Whips a heavy lefty forehand with a semi-western grip and a lot of shoulder rotation, often hitting it on the run or while airborne.
Comfortable coming forward behind the serve, using his athleticism and reach to cover the net and finish with volleys and overheads.

lesson: Serve power comes from the legs: bend deep and drive up into the ball.

name: Lorenzo Musetti

techniqueNotes.note: A flowing one-hander with a high, elaborate take-back, a full shoulder turn and an extended, straight-arm contact in front; he can generate winners from deep behind the baseline or wide outside the doubles alley.
Uses a continental-grip backhand slice with a high-to-low path and long follow-through to defend, change rhythm and keep the ball low, often preparing identically for the slice and the drop shot.
Plays the drop shot off the same slice preparation, softening the grip and shortening the follow-through so opponents cannot read it early.

lesson: Prepare the same way for slice, drop shot and drive so your variety is disguised.

name: Iga Swiatek

techniqueNotes.note: Uses a western grip, rare on the WTA, with a steep upward swing that produces topspin rates comparable to the men's tour; the ball clears the net high and kicks up sharply, especially on clay.
Slides into shots on both clay and hard courts from a low, wide base and recovers with explosive crossover steps, so she is set early enough to attack from defensive positions.
Steps well inside the baseline to return second serves, taking the ball early with a compact swing to immediately pressure the server.

lesson: Heavy topspin plus elite movement lets you attack with margin.

name: Aryna Sabalenka

techniqueNotes.note: Hits with a semi-western grip, a big shoulder turn and full-body rotation, averaging forehand speeds comparable to top ATP players; she commits to the swing and aims big to large targets rather than the lines.
Rebuilt her serve with a biomechanics coach after a period of double faults, stabilizing the toss position and simplifying the rhythm so the motion holds up under pressure.
Drives a flat, heavy two-hander with long extension, equally willing to go down the line as cross-court.

lesson: Technical flaws can be fixed: rebuild the fundamentals (toss, rhythm) and power becomes reliable.

name: Elena Rybakina

techniqueNotes.note: At 1.84 m she uses a relaxed, effortless-looking motion with a smooth tempo, a toss in front and full extension at contact, producing the biggest first serve on the WTA and regularly leading the tour in aces.
Hits flat and clean with a calm, simple take-back and little wasted motion, stepping into the ball and driving through it rather than brushing up.
A flat, linear two-hander with early preparation and long extension; she takes it early and redirects down the line with the same swing.

lesson: Effortless power comes from relaxed, simple technique and clean timing, not from muscling the ball.

name: Ashleigh Barty

techniqueNotes.note: Her backhand slice is the best of her generation: continental grip, full shoulder turn, racquet starting above the ball and carving high-to-low with a long follow-through while staying sideways, keeping the ball skidding below the opponent's knees.
Only 1.66 m tall but among the WTA ace leaders thanks to precise placement, a strong leg drive and heavy slice and kick variations rather than raw speed.
Hits a heavy-topspin forehand with a semi-western grip and uses the low slice to draw short balls she can run around and attack with it.

lesson: A low, biting slice changes the rhythm of a rally and sets up your attacking shots.

name: Coco Gauff

techniqueNotes.note: Her two-hander is her most reliable weapon: compact take-back, early contact in front and firm through the hitting zone, struck from open or closed stance and redirected down the line with ease.
One of the fastest players on tour; she defends from a wide open stance, sliding into shots and recovering fast enough to turn defense into offense.

Uses an extreme western-leaning grip with a long swing, which produces heavy spin but makes low or fast balls harder to time; a useful example of how extreme grips trade consistency under pressure for spin.

lesson: Build your game around your most reliable shot and let your movement cover the rest.

name: Naomi Osaka

techniqueNotes.note: Generates first serves near 200 km/h with a smooth motion, a deep knee bend and strong upward leg drive, hitting flat to both corners to win free points.
Hits from an open stance with a semi-western grip, big hip and shoulder rotation and a flat, heavy ball, looking to strike first from the baseline.
Drives a flat two-hander with good extension, particularly strong cross-court and on the return of serve.

lesson: First-strike tennis: a big serve followed by a committed first forehand.

name: Barbora Krejcikova

techniqueNotes.note: A former doubles world No. 1 whose net skills carry into singles: continental grip, compact punch with almost no backswing, and a forward-moving split step that lets her close and angle volleys away.
Mixes backhand slices and changes of pace into baseline rallies to break the rhythm of harder hitters and create short balls to approach on.
Uses soft hands and a late grip change to play disguised drop shots, then follows them forward to cover the reply at net.

lesson: Doubles skills such as volleys, touch and variety win singles points too.

name: Madison Keys

techniqueNotes.note: One of the hardest forehands in women's tennis: a semi-western grip, a full unit turn, pronounced racquet lag and very fast racquet-head speed through contact, hit from a loaded open stance.
A powerful first serve from a fluid motion with a strong leg drive; late in her career she adjusted equipment and technique for more control and margin rather than more pace.
Hits a heavy two-hander with full rotation and is willing to change direction down the line early in the rally.

lesson: Raw power becomes a winning weapon once you add margin and shot selection to it.

name: Mirra Andreeva

techniqueNotes.note: A compact, early-prepared two-hander that she redirects down the line with the same swing, using clean timing and contact in front rather than a large backswing.
Blends drop shots, slices and lobs into baseline rallies with soft hands, choosing them when the opponent is pushed deep so the variety is tactical rather than decorative.
Reads the serve early and returns deep with a short swing, starting points on neutral or better against bigger servers.

lesson: Tactical variety and good shot selection can beat bigger hitters at any age.

name: Ons Jabeur

techniqueNotes.note: The most prolific drop-shotter of her era: she sets up with a normal forehand or backhand preparation, changes to a continental grip late and cuts under the ball with an open face and relaxed hand, adding sidespin so the ball moves away after the bounce.
Uses forehand and backhand slices to change pace and height, keeping the ball low and forcing opponents to generate their own pace.
Varies the forehand between a flat drive, a heavy topspin roll and sharp short angles, all from similar preparation, so opponents cannot settle into a rhythm.

lesson: Disguise comes from identical preparation: make your drop shot look like your drive until the last moment.
